flags.heading: A Guide Sent in Disguise
flags.text: The Book of Tobit tells of an elderly, devout Israelite named Tobit, struck blind, who sends his son Tobias on a long journey to recover a sum of money owed to him.

flags.heading: A Guide Sent in Disguise
flags.text: Throughout the journey Raphael instructs Tobias in small, practical particulars — how to catch and prepare a certain fish, what its organs are good for — offering no hint of anything miraculous, simply the quiet, patient counsel of an experienced companion.

flags.heading: Healing Two Households at Once
flags.text: It is a double miracle that Raphael accomplishes not by a single dramatic act, but through ordinary remedies, faithfully explained in advance to those who trusted him enough to follow his instructions exactly.

flags.heading: Patron of Every Ordinary Journey
flags.text: Some later commentators have further identified Raphael with the unnamed angel of the Lord who is said, in John's Gospel, to trouble the healing waters of the pool of Bethesda (John 5:4 in some manuscript traditions).

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Raphael remains the patron most often invoked by travelers setting out on a journey, the sick seeking healing, and those who hope, like Tobias and Sara before them, for a marriage delivered from whatever threatens it.

flags.heading: A Mother Chosen Twice
flags.text: Born Zoé Labouré on 2 May 1806 at Fain-lès-Moutiers in Burgundy, the ninth of eleven surviving children of a prosperous farmer and his devout wife, Catherine lost her mother, Madeleine, when she was only nine years old.

flags.heading: A Mother Chosen Twice
flags.text: Returning from the funeral, she is remembered as having taken up a small statue of Our Lady from the family mantel, held it close, and said, "Now, dear Blessed Virgin, you will be my mother" — a child's vow that would prove, in the end, no passing grief but the whole shape of a life.

flags.heading: A Farmhouse, Not a Schoolroom
flags.text: With her mother gone and her older sisters married or already in religious life, the household fell to Catherine, who at only twelve took charge of her father's farm kitchen and its brood of younger siblings, receiving almost no formal schooling in the years that followed.

flags.heading: A Farmhouse, Not a Schoolroom
flags.text: When she confided at eighteen that she wished to enter the convent, her father refused outright and sent her instead to work as a waitress in an uncle's café in Paris, hoping the city's distractions would quiet a vocation he could not understand.

flags.heading: A Farmhouse, Not a Schoolroom
flags.text: Catherine remained as set on religious life amid the noise of the café as she had been in her father's quiet kitchen, and an aunt's steady intercession eventually won her father's reluctant consent.

flags.heading: A Priest Seen Before He Was Known
flags.text: Some years before that consent came, Catherine reported a vivid dream of an elderly priest beckoning her toward a room full of the sick, telling her, "It is a good deed to look after the sick.

flags.heading: A Priest Seen Before He Was Known
flags.text: She recognized his face only later, and by surprise, in a portrait hanging on the wall of a Daughters of Charity hospital: it was St. Vincent de Paul, dead for over a century and a half, whose own daughters she would soon join.

flags.heading: A Priest Seen Before He Was Known
flags.text: In January 1830, at twenty-three, Catherine entered the novitiate of the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul, arriving that April at the community's motherhouse on the Rue du Bac in Paris — the very convent where, within months, her hidden life would be interrupted by visions no one could have prepared her for.

flags.heading: The Virgin in the Motherhouse Chapel
flags.text: On the night of 18–19 July 1830, a child's voice woke Catherine and led her to the convent chapel, where she found the Blessed Virgin seated near the sanctuary and kept vigil at her feet for hours, hearing a warning of coming trials for France and for the Church that seemed, within days, confirmed by the revolution that broke out across Paris that same July.

flags.heading: The Virgin in the Motherhouse Chapel
flags.text: On 27 November of that same year, in the same chapel, Mary appeared to her again, standing on a globe with rays of light streaming from her hands, framed by an oval bearing the words "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee," and instructed Catherine to have a medal struck to this exact design.

flags.heading: A Medal, and a Silence Kept for Life
flags.text: Catherine confided everything to her confessor, the Vincentian priest Fr. Jean-Marie Aladel, who doubted her account for nearly two years before finally seeking the Archbishop of Paris's permission to have the medal struck in 1832.

flags.heading: A Medal, and a Silence Kept for Life
flags.text: What became known almost at once as the Miraculous Medal spread across France and then the world with extraordinary speed, credited within its first years with a great many reported healings and conversions — yet Catherine herself asked that her own identity as the visionary be kept secret, and Fr. Aladel honored that request until shortly before his own death.

flags.heading: A Medal, and a Silence Kept for Life
flags.text: Appointed after her formation to the community's hospice at Enghien-Reuilly, on the edge of Paris, Catherine spent the remaining forty-six years of her religious life there in unbroken obscurity — tending the elderly and infirm, keeping the poultry yard, answering the convent gate — known to her own sisters only as a quiet, faithful, rather unremarkable member of the community.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Only in the final months of her life, in 1876, did Catherine finally reveal her secret, telling her superior plainly that she believed she would not live to see another Christmas and that the truth could not be buried with her.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: She died at Enghien-Reuilly on 31 December 1876, seventy years old, and when her body was exhumed in 1933 in the course of her cause for canonization, it was found remarkably incorrupt, still resting today beneath the same chapel on the Rue du Bac where she had once knelt before the Virgin as an anonymous young novice.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Beatified in 1933 and canonized in 1947 by Pope Pius XII, Catherine Labouré is remembered by the Church less for the brilliance of her visions than for the forty-six ordinary, hidden years that followed them — a life that helped prepare the ground for the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854 and, in time, for Lourdes itself, and that still says to every believer tempted to think their own hidden faithfulness goes unnoticed: it does not.

flags.heading: A Name Without a Story
flags.text: Tertullian, writing around the year 199, records the tradition that Clement was ordained a bishop by St. Peter himself, and St. Jerome tells us that in his own day ‘most of the Latins’ believed the same.

flags.heading: A Name Without a Story
flags.text: Whatever the precise sequence, the ancient Church remembered Clement as standing close enough to the apostles to have their voices still ringing in his ears — a living bridge, however faint the record of him has become, between the world of the Twelve and the world that came after them.

flags.heading: A Letter to a Divided Church
flags.text: Word of the crisis reached Rome, and Clement, writing in the name of ‘the church of God which sojourns at Rome’ to ‘the church of God sojourning at Corinth,’ answered with a document of real pastoral authority — reasoning from Scripture and from Christ's own humility that ministers appointed by the apostles, and by their orderly successors, may not be removed at a faction's whim.

flags.heading: Rome's First Word to a Sister Church
flags.text: What strikes the careful reader is less any single argument than the letter's tone: a church far from Corinth writes as though it has every right to be heard, and Corinth, remarkably, listened.

flags.heading: Rome's First Word to a Sister Church
flags.text: Even so, here, in one of Christianity's earliest surviving documents outside Scripture, is Rome already speaking to a sister church with a confidence that the apostolic ministry it defends is not Corinth's alone to unmake — an early, often-noted witness to how quickly the Roman church came to feel responsible for the peace of the wider body of Christ.

flags.heading: A Legend of Exile and the Sea
flags.text: The vivid story later ages told — exile to a Crimean quarry under Trajan, a miraculous spring struck from rock, and finally martyrdom by drowning with an anchor bound to his neck — is exactly that: a later story.

flags.heading: A Legend of Exile and the Sea
flags.text: The Catholic Encyclopedia states plainly that the account cannot be traced earlier than the fourth century, and the two writers closest to Clement's own era, Eusebius and Jerome, say nothing at all of any martyrdom.

flags.heading: A Legend of Exile and the Sea
flags.text: What can be said is that by the sixth century the tradition was well established, and that in the ninth century Sts. Cyril and Methodius carried relics believed to be Clement's own to Rome, where they rest beneath the ancient basilica of San Clemente that still bears his name.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Every pastor who has ever had to write a hard letter to a community not his own, trusting truth spoken in love to be received, finds in Clement an unlikely companion — a man history remembers less for who he was than for what he was willing to say.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Church keeps his feast on November 23 and honors him, through the anchor of his legend, as a patron of mariners: fitting enough for a shepherd whose one sure legacy is a single letter that, after nineteen centuries, still holds.

flags.heading: A Reluctant Soldier's Conversion
flags.text: At twenty he was seized for the army, one of many young Egyptians conscripted to serve the Emperor Constantine's campaigns, and shipped downriver under guard with other frightened recruits who had no idea what awaited them.

flags.heading: A Vision at Tabennisi
flags.text: Pachomius, staying for a time at the deserted village of Tabennisi on the Nile's east bank, believed he received a vision there commanding him to remain and build not another hermitage but a monastery — a house where many could live the ascetic life together.

flags.heading: A Vision at Tabennisi
flags.text: It was a genuinely new proposal: rather than each man wrestling alone in his own cave, monks would share meals, labor, and the hours of prayer, held together by a common rule rather than each hermit's private discipline.

flags.heading: A Rule for the Common Life
flags.text: The move from solitary to shared life did not come easily even to those who wanted it — early companions, formed only in the eremitical ideal, chafed at meals in common and organized labor.

flags.heading: A Rule for the Common Life
flags.text: Out of this experience he drew up what is generally recognized as the first written rule for cenobitic, or communal, monastic life — a structured pattern of prayer, work, and common meals that could be taught to hundreds rather than handed down one hermit to one disciple.

flags.heading: A Rule for the Common Life
flags.text: The rule spread with startling speed: by the time of Pachomius's death, the monastery at Tabennisi had grown into eleven communities in all, nine for men and two for women, following his pattern along the Nile.

flags.heading: Father of a New Kind of Monk
flags.text: St. Anthony of Egypt, whose solitary combat in the desert had already made him famous, represented one great model of Christian asceticism — the hermit alone with God; Pachomius, his younger contemporary, offered another, no less demanding but built for the many rather than the few.

flags.heading: Father of a New Kind of Monk
flags.text: Both models flowed, decades later, into the monastic legislation of St. Basil the Great in the East and, still later, into the Rule St. Benedict of Nursia composed for the West, which owed a real, if indirect, debt to the discipline Pachomius worked out at Tabennisi two centuries before.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: He shows every Christian who has ever tried to build something larger than personal virtue — a parish, a family, a community of any kind — that holiness is rarely only a private matter between one soul and God.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: It is also a patient, unglamorous work of learning to live well with others: sharing labor, bearing with the slow and the stubborn, building structures sturdy enough to outlast their founder.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The monk who once thought only of surviving the army now stands, however unlikely it once seemed, as the father of an entire way of Christian life still practiced, in spirit if not in every particular, wherever men and women vow to seek God not alone but together.

flags.heading: A Child of the Frontier
flags.text: Internal evidence from his own writings suggests his family was already Christian, though later biographers, perhaps to heighten the drama of his conversion, claimed his father served as a pagan priest.

flags.heading: A Child of the Frontier
flags.text: He was baptized in his youth and came under the guidance of St. James, bishop of Nisibis and one of the bishops who had sat at the Council of Nicaea I a generation earlier.

flags.heading: A Child of the Frontier
flags.text: Under James's care Ephrem grew into a teacher at the school of Nisibis, and it was there, amid the daily pressure of a garrison city on the Persian frontier, that he began the work of writing that would occupy the rest of his life.

flags.heading: Songs Against Heresy
flags.text: It sat in the path of Persian invasion, and its Christians lived amid the pull of rival teachers — Gnostics, Marcionites, and the followers of the poet-philosopher Bardaisan, who had discovered that beautiful music spreads doctrine, true or false, more effectively than any lecture.

flags.heading: Songs Against Heresy
flags.text: Ephrem's answer was to meet them on their own ground: rather than dense refutations few would read, he composed hymns of his own, doctrinally precise and set to melodies the whole congregation could sing, and by his own account 'clothed' sound teaching in the same 'garment of musical beauty' heretics had used to dress up their errors.

flags.heading: Exile to Edessa
flags.text: In 363 the Emperor Jovian, forced to buy peace after a disastrous war, ceded Nisibis outright to Persia, and its Christian population, Ephrem among them, fled west into Roman territory rather than live under a hostile king.

flags.heading: Exile to Edessa
flags.text: Later Syrian biographers add a journey to visit St. Basil the Great at Caesarea, and even an ordination as deacon at Basil's hands — a tradition repeated by reliable ancient authors, though some modern critics judge the evidence insufficient and set it aside.

flags.heading: Exile to Edessa
flags.text: What is certain is that Ephrem, though he wrote no Greek, was already revered across confessional lines in his own lifetime, Orthodox, Monophysite, and Nestorian Syriac Christians alike claiming him for their own long after his death.

flags.heading: Death Among the Plague-Stricken
flags.text: Edessa suffered a severe famine in 372 and 373, and Ephrem, by then an old man, threw himself into organizing relief for the starving city — distributing grain, tending plague victims, and, by tradition, contracting the illness that killed him from the very sick he had gone to serve.

flags.heading: Death Among the Plague-Stricken
flags.text: He died in June of 373, having spent a life that began under siege and ended in service to the dying, without ever once, so far as the record shows, seeking safety over duty.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Pope Benedict XV declared Ephrem a Doctor of the Universal Church in 1920 — the only Syriac writer and the only deacon ever to receive the honor, a recognition that came fifteen centuries after his death but corrected no error in judgment, only a long delay in the West's attention to the East.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: We recognize in Ephrem something every believer facing a world of noisy, competing voices still needs: the conviction that beauty is not opposed to truth but can carry it, that a hymn sung by ordinary people in the pews may do more to hold the faith together than an argument understood only by scholars.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: The Church still prays his short Lenten prayer for purity of heart across the Christian East to this day, a fittingly humble monument for a man who, the ancient sources agree, never once quoted his own name in his own writing — content to let the song outlast the singer.

flags.heading: A Young Man's Pilgrimage East
flags.text: Cassian was born around the year 360; the ancient biographer Gennadius calls him a Scythian by birth, and much recent scholarship follows that lead and places his childhood in Scythia Minor, in the region of modern Romania, though older studies argued instead for a birth in Roman Gaul.

flags.heading: A Young Man's Pilgrimage East
flags.text: Whatever his native country, he received the education of a young man of means and, still young, traveled with a close friend named Germanus to see the holy places of Palestine.

flags.heading: A Young Man's Pilgrimage East
flags.text: Drawn by reports of the holiness of the desert fathers, Cassian and Germanus left for Egypt and did not return for seven years, wandering from one renowned ascetic to another, gathering in memory the sayings and disciplines that would later fill his two great books.

flags.heading: Among the Desert Fathers
flags.text: For roughly fifteen years, on and off, Cassian and Germanus lived among the solitaries of the Egyptian desert, most famously in the region of Scetis, absorbing a tradition of prayer and self-discipline already a century old by the time St. Anthony of Egypt had made it famous.

flags.heading: Among the Desert Fathers
flags.text: When Chrysostom was driven from his see in 404, Cassian journeyed to Rome to plead his mentor's cause before the pope — the last clearly documented event of the next decade of his life, after which the record falls silent until he resurfaces, a priest now, in southern Gaul.

flags.heading: A Monastery at Marseilles
flags.text: Around the year 415 Cassian settled at Marseilles and founded two monasteries on the model he had studied in Egypt, one for men built over the tomb of the martyr St. Victor and one for women — among the first such houses in the Latin West.

flags.heading: A Monastery at Marseilles
flags.text: To instruct his new communities, largely ignorant of the Eastern tradition he had lived so long, he wrote the Institutes, describing the practical shape of monastic life, and then the Conferences, presenting the deeper teaching of the desert fathers as extended dialogues.

flags.heading: A Monastery at Marseilles
flags.text: St. Benedict himself, writing his own Rule roughly a century later, ordered that selections from the Conferences be read daily in his monasteries, calling the work a 'mirror of monastic life' — clear evidence of how completely Cassian's transplanted wisdom had taken root in the West.

flags.heading: A Contested Legacy
flags.text: Writing as the West absorbed the implications of St. Augustine's teaching on grace and predestination, Cassian argued for a position — later labeled semi-Pelagian by theologians who came after him — that stressed the human will's first, faltering movement toward God alongside grace's necessity for everything that followed.

flags.heading: A Contested Legacy
flags.text: The Church would side more fully with Augustine's account of grace at the Second Council of Orange in 529, decades after Cassian's death, and theologians have debated ever since how fair that later label really was to what Cassian meant.

flags.heading: A Contested Legacy
flags.text: He also wrote, near the end of his life, a treatise defending the Council of Ephesus's condemnation of Nestorius — proof the old monk of Marseilles was still tracking the great doctrinal battles of his age.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Cassian died around the year 435, and though the formal process of canonization did not yet exist to make his sainthood official, the Church of Marseilles has kept his feast without interruption ever since, and Pope Urban V — himself once abbot of the monastery Cassian founded — had the word 'Saint' engraved on the reliquary holding his head.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: We recognize in Cassian a patient teacher who understood that no one arrives at contemplative stillness by willpower alone; the eight besetting faults he catalogued for his monks, from gluttony to pride, remain a strikingly accurate map of the obstacles between any human heart and the God it is trying to reach.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Every believer who has tried to build a disciplined life of prayer and found himself undone by the very faults Cassian named owes an old, largely unacknowledged debt to the wandering scholar who carried the desert home to the West.

flags.heading: A Deacon Elevated
flags.text: Peter was born in Imola, in the Roman province of Aemilia, in the last years of the fourth century — ancient sources vary on the exact date, some placing his birth around 380, others closer to 400.

flags.heading: A Deacon Elevated
flags.text: Around 433, Pope Sixtus III consecrated Peter bishop of Ravenna, then serving as the seat of the Western Roman emperors — apparently setting aside the candidate the Ravennese clergy and people had themselves elected, a highly unusual intervention later biographers explained, though without contemporary confirmation, by a vision guiding the pope's hand.

flags.heading: The Golden-Worded
flags.text: The name Chrysologus, 'golden word,' was almost certainly bestowed on Peter in his own century, likely by the imperial court, in deliberate echo of the great Eastern preacher St. John Chrysostom, whose name meant the same.

flags.heading: The Golden-Worded
flags.text: Peter earned it not through length but economy: his surviving sermons, some 176 collected in later centuries, run only a few minutes each, and he told his congregation plainly that he kept them short out of respect for their attention rather than any shortage of things to say.

flags.heading: The Golden-Worded
flags.text: With the backing of the empress-regent Galla Placidia, who governed in the name of her young son Valentinian III, Peter built and adorned churches across Ravenna and worked steadily to root out the last vestiges of pagan practice among his people, cautioning them, in sermons that survive to this day, against indecent public dancing and old superstitions dressed up as harmless custom.

flags.heading: A Steadying Voice in a Doctrinal Storm
flags.text: In 448 the Eastern monk Eutyches was condemned by a synod at Constantinople for teaching that Christ possessed only a single, divine nature after the Incarnation — the heresy that would come to be called Monophysitism.

flags.heading: A Steadying Voice in a Doctrinal Storm
flags.text: Peter's reply survives among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon: he withheld his own judgment on the theological question and instead firmly instructed Eutyches to submit to Rome's authority and accept whatever Pope Leo determined.

flags.heading: A Steadying Voice in a Doctrinal Storm
flags.text: It was a small act with large consequences — a bishop of no great see using his personal credibility not to build a faction of his own but to point a wavering churchman back toward unity, in the very years the whole controversy was moving toward the ecumenical council that would settle it three years later.

flags.heading: Death and a Quiet Homecoming
flags.text: Peter died around the year 450, according to tradition at Imola, the small town of his birth, to which he had returned near the end of his life to venerate the relics of St. Cassian of Imola.

flags.heading: Death and a Quiet Homecoming
flags.text: Ancient accounts, more devotional than strictly verifiable, describe him making a final offering at that shrine and commending his soul, through the martyr's intercession, before he died — a fittingly modest close for a bishop whose entire pastoral method had been built on brevity and humility rather than display.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: It was not until 1729, nearly thirteen centuries after his death, that Pope Benedict XIII named Peter Chrysologus a Doctor of the Church — recognition, astonishingly overdue, of sermons their own author had insisted were too brief to matter much beyond the moment of their preaching.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: He shows every preacher, and indeed every believer who has ever worried that they have too little to offer, that faithfulness in small and disciplined acts — a few honest minutes of teaching, a letter written to steady a wavering friend rather than to win an argument — can outlast empires built on far grander ambitions.

flags.heading: Legacy
flags.text: Ravenna's empire is gone; the golden-worded bishop's plain, short sermons on prayer, fasting, and mercy are still read, not least his own most quoted words: 'Fasting is the soul of prayer, almsgiving is the lifeblood of fasting.'

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: An Irish nobleman who traded a life of comfort for the wandering life of a monk, Columbanus set out from Bangor Abbey with twelve companions determined to bring Irish monastic rigor to a continental Church he judged badly in need of reform.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: He founded Luxeuil in the forests of Gaul and, when his blunt criticism of the Frankish court's morals finally cost him that monastery, pressed on through Switzerland into northern Italy rather than turn back.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: He was never formally canonized in a Church that had not yet developed the process, yet Rome has kept his feast for over a thousand years, and Pope Benedict XVI would later call him, simply, 'a European saint.'

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Born Hildebrand to a family of humble standing in Tuscany, Gregory VII spent decades as the power behind several popes before he was himself acclaimed pope by the shouting of the Roman crowd at Gregory VI's funeral.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: He devoted his pontificate to a single, relentless purpose: freeing the Church from the control of kings and nobles who bought and sold bishoprics as if they were parcels of land.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: His standoff with the German Emperor Henry IV produced one of the most famous scenes of the Middle Ages, when the humbled emperor stood barefoot in the snow outside the castle of Canossa begging absolution.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: A Dutch student who joined the newly founded Society of Jesus in its earliest years, Peter Canisius became, almost single-handedly, the public face of the Catholic response to the Reformation across the German-speaking lands.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: He walked or rode an estimated twenty thousand miles over thirty years, preaching, founding colleges, and writing a catechism so clear and so widely translated that it shaped Catholic religious instruction for centuries after his death.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: He represented the Church's interests at the Council of Trent and at difficult public conferences with Protestant theologians, always preferring, by his own account, to explain the faith's abiding truth rather than simply denounce his opponents' errors.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Orphaned by twelve and turned away from job after job by a body too frail for ordinary labor, Alfred Bessette seemed an unlikely candidate when he asked to join the Congregation of Holy Cross in Montreal, carrying only a note from his old pastor that read, 'I am sending you a saint.'

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Assigned the lowly post of doorkeeper at a college for more than forty years, Brother André spent his days praying with the sick and the desperate who came to him, attributing every healing that followed not to himself but to St. Joseph, to whom he had a lifelong devotion.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Out of nickel haircuts and small donations he raised, against every expectation, the funds to begin what would become Saint Joseph's Oratory, now one of the largest shrines in the world.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: When he died in 1937, nearly a million mourners filed past his body in the depths of a Quebec winter, and in 2010 he became the first Canadian-born man to be declared a saint.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: A watchmaker who had once been turned away from the monastery and a lacemaker who had once been turned away from the convent, Louis and Zélie Martin found in each other, and then in marriage itself, the vocation to holiness each had originally sought elsewhere.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Married in 1858 after a courtship of only a few months, they raised nine children in a home saturated with ordinary daily prayer, sending five surviving daughters into religious life, including the youngest, whom the world would come to know as St. Thérèse of Lisieux.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: Zélie died of breast cancer in 1877, and Louis, after years of failing health that included a difficult stay in a sanitarium, followed her in 1894 — leaving behind not a single dramatic public deed but an entire household formed, letter by letter and habit by habit, into a school of sanctity.

flags.heading: Overview
flags.text: In 2015 Pope Francis canonized them together, the first married couple in history to be declared saints as a couple, holding up their home in Alençon and Lisieux as proof that ordinary family life, rightly lived, is itself a genuine path to God.
